prompt:
A CI dashboard shows "Not all tests passed". Writing P(t) for "test t passed", which statement is equivalent? Assume all tests have completed and each result is pass or fail.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: for every t not P(t): every test failed
options.explanation: This pushes the ¬ inside without flipping the quantifier. "Not all passed" is consistent with 99 of 100 passing.

options.text: not there exists t P(t): no test passed
options.explanation: This is equivalent to "every test failed", the same over-strong reading as the first option.

options.text: there exists t not P(t): at least one test failed
options.explanation: Correct. not for every t P(t) is equivalent to there exists t not P(t). One failing test is enough to make "all passed" false.

options.text: there exists t P(t): at least one test passed
options.explanation: This doesn't negate anything; it is compatible with every test passing, which the dashboard rules out.

workedExample:
1. The dashboard says "not all tests passed".
2. Apply the quantifier De Morgan law: flip ∀ to ∃ and move ¬ inside.

```formula
¬∀t P(t) ≡ ∃t ¬P(t)
where
t: a variable ranging over the tests in the run
P(t): the predicate "test t passed"
¬: NOT
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not every test passed" means "some test did not pass".
```

3. On a finite suite of three tests it is the propositional De Morgan law you already know:

```formula
¬(P_1 ∧ P_2 ∧ P_3) ≡ ¬P_1 ∨ ¬P_2 ∨ ¬P_3
where
P_1, P_2, P_3: "test 1 passed", "test 2 passed", "test 3 passed"
¬: NOT
∧: AND: true only when every part is true
∨: OR: true when at least one part is true
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not all three passed" is "test 1 failed, or test 2 failed, or test 3 failed".
```

prompt:
Which of these are correct negations of for every x (A(x) implies B(x))? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means OR (inclusive); → means "implies" (if ... then); ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: there exists x (A(x) and not B(x))
options.explanation: Correct. Flip ∀ to ∃ and negate the inside: "not (if A then B)" is "A and not B".

options.text: for every x (A(x) implies not B(x))
options.explanation: This says no A is a B. It is not equivalent to the negation: with no A objects it is vacuously true, while not-every-A-is-B is false. If A objects exist, it requires all of them to fail B rather than just one.

options.text: there exists x not (not A(x) or B(x))
options.explanation: Correct. "If A then B" is the same as "not A or B", so this is "there is an x where (if A then B) fails", the negation. It simplifies to the first option.

options.text: there exists x (A(x) implies not B(x))
options.explanation: This negates only the consequent. It is true whenever some x is not an A (vacuous truth), so it is not the negation.

workedExample:
Push the negation inside one step at a time:

```formula
¬∀x (A(x) → B(x))
  ≡ ∃x ¬(A(x) → B(x))
  ≡ ∃x ¬(¬A(x) ∨ B(x))
  ≡ ∃x (¬¬A(x) ∧ ¬B(x))
  ≡ ∃x (A(x) ∧ ¬B(x))
where
x: a variable ranging over the domain
A(x), B(x): predicates, true or false for each x
¬: NOT; ¬¬A(x) is NOT applied twice, which gives A(x) back
→: implies: false only when the left side is true and the right side false
∨: OR
∧: AND
∀: for all
∃: there exists at least one
≡: is logically equivalent to
In words: "not every A is a B" means "some A is not a B". The third line is option C and the last line is option A.
```

Note the result uses ∧, matching the rule that ∃ pairs with ∧.
